documentation.range: The Smallspotted Catshark is found in the Northeast and Eastern Central Atlantic Ocean (from Norway and the British Isles to Senegal and possibly Benin) and the Mediterranean Sea, including the Black Sea (Ebert et al. 2013).
documentation.population:
The Smallspotted Catshark is considered common and one of the most abundant elasmobranchs across its range in the Northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea (ICES-WGEF 2019, Ramírez-Amaro et al. 2020).

Species-specific population trend data are available from standardized catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE) in the Northeast Atlantic and the Mediterranean Sea (Serena 2014, ICES-WGEF 2019, Ramírez-Amaro et al. 2020). The trend data were analysed over three generation lengths (39 years) using a Bayesian state-space framework (Sherley et al. 2020, Winker et al. 2020). This analysis yields an annual rate of change, a median change over three generation lengths, and the probability of the most likely IUCN Red List category percent change over three generations (see the Supplementary Information). The trend analysis of the CPUE from trawl survey in the Irish Sea and Bristol Channel revealed an annual rate of increase of 3.7% and an increasing population over three generation lengths (39 years). The relative abundance estimates from the Mediterranean International Trawl Survey (MEDITS) in the Western Mediterranean Sea (Northern Alboran Sea, off the Balearic Islands and Northern Spain, 1994–2015), and Central Mediterranean Sea and Adriatic Sea (1994–2011) revealed an annual rate of increase of 6.6% and an increasing population over three generation lengths (39 years). The global weighted trend estimated a 356% population increase over three generation lengths (39 years). The data were estimated to represent 92% of the species' known spatial distribution.

Across West Africa, total artisanal fishing effort increased by 10-fold between 1950 and 2010, while the catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE) of artisanal and industrial vessels declined by 34% over this period (Belhabib et al. 2018). While these levels of change are not species-specific, they are informative for understanding the broader levels of decline in marine fish in the region. The Smallspotted Catshark was rarely reported in Mauritania and Senegal during landing site surveys across the Sub-Regional Fisheries Commission region between 2004 and 2011 (Diop and Dossa 2011), and may have some refuge with depth in this region.

Across the regions, the Smallspotted Catshark was estimated to have increased in the Northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea, and suspected to be stable in the Eastern Central Atlantic. The species is not suspected to be close to reaching the population reduction threshold. There is nothing to suspect or infer population reduction at this time, and the Smallspotted Catshark is assessed as Least Concern.
documentation.habitats: The Smallspotted Catshark is demersal on the continental shelf and upper slope from nearshore to a depth of 800 m (Weigmann 2016). It is reported to reach a maximum size of 100 cm total length (TL) in the Atlantic (Ebert et al. 2013, Weigmann 2016), but it generally attains a maximum of 80 cm TL, and larger specimens may relate to misidentified with the Nursehound (S. stellaris) (Ellis 2015). It attains a smaller maximum size (60 cm TL) in the Mediterranean Sea. In the Atlantic, males mature at 53.5 cm TL and females mature at 57 cm TL; in the Mediterranean Sea, males mature at 39 cm TL and females mature at 44 cm TL (Ivory et al. 2005, Ebert et al. 2013, Soares and de Carvalho 2019). Reproduction is oviparous, with egg cases laid year-round and size-at-birth is 9–10 cm TL (Ebert et al. 2013, Soares and de Carvalho 2019). In the Atlantic, estimated female age-at-maturity is 9 years and maximum age is 17 years, resulting in a generation length of 13 years (Rodríguez-Cabello et al. 2005b).
documentation.threats:
The Smallspotted Catshark is reported as incidental catch in bottom trawl, longline, and gillnet fisheries across its range (ICES-WGEF 2019). The Northeast Atlantic and the Mediterranean have been subject to extensive and intensive fishing across much of the species' known depth and spatial distribution (Ellis et al. 2009). In the Mediterranean Sea, relative abundance of the Smallspotted Catshark was highest at depths of 400–500 m (Ragonese et al. 2013). Despite a number of management measures to reduce deep-water shark fishing mortality, the species is still captured in demersal fisheries (e.g. Moura et al. 2018). Discard mortality is estimated to be very low (Rodríguez-Cabello et al. 2005a, Ellis et al. 2017). 

In the Eastern Central Atlantic, sharks and rays were already being exploited by semi-industrial fisheries in the 1950s (Walker et al. 2005). While these fisheries gradually collapsed, the demand for dried salted shark meat (for export to Ghana) and shark fins in the 1980s drove the development of artisanal targeted shark fishing across much of the region (Diop and Dossa 2011, CCLME 2016, Seto et al. 2017, Moore et al. 2019). Over the years, this has expanded into targeted shark and ray fisheries across many countries and is likely increasing fishing pressure on this species (Walker et al. 2005, Diop and Dossa 2011). The Smallspotted Catshark was rarely reported from fisheries operating in Mauritania and Senegal (Diop and Dossa 2011).

There are currently three active mixed fishery bilateral agreements between the European Union and the West African nations of Morocco, Mauritania, and Guinea-Bissau (European Commission 2020). These agreements, known as Sustainable Fisheries Partnership Agreements (SFPAs) involve payments to third party countries in exchange for access to marine resources and sectorial support aimed at promoting sustainable fisheries development in the partner countries. Under SFPAs, there are a number of European distant-water industrial vessels using demersal trawls to capture deep-water shrimps at depths of 400–950 m in Mauritania and demersal trawl fisheries for black hake (Merluccius senegalensis and Merluccius polli) operate mainly at depths 500–700 m (Fernandez Peralta et al. 2019). In the Mauritanian trawl fisheries, unidentified deep-water sharks and rays have accounted for approximately 10% of landings (Fernandez Peralta et al. 2019). Bottom trawl and longline fisheries in southern Morocco target a number of demersal fish, including black hake and scabbardfish. Trawl fishing here occurs mostly at depths 500–800 m and longline fishing occurs at 100–400 m (Cervantes et al. 2018). Further information on bycatch species in these fisheries is largely unknown.
documentation.measures:
Further information is required on population size and trends of the Smallspotted Catshark, as well as interactions with fisheries across its range, particularly around West Africa. There are some general management arrangements of relevance in place in the Northeast Atlantic, including minimum mesh sizes for targeting Scyliorhinus spp. (EC Reg 850/98 of 30 March 1998).

Management measures for deep-water sharks in European Community waters may offer some refuge for the Smallspotted Catshark at the deeper end of its bathymetric distribution. These management measures include banned use of trawls and gillnets in waters >200 m depth in Azores, Madeira and Canary Islands and international waters regulated by ICES (NEAFC regulatory Area); banned use of gillnets by European Union vessels at depths >600 m; maximum bycatch limits of deep-water shark in Hake (Merluccius merluccius) and monkfish (Lophius spp) gillnet catches; area restrictions by vessel size and gear, gear restrictions (hook size, maximum number of hooks on longline gear), and a network of closed areas in Azorean waters; closure of the Condor seamount to deep-water fishing in 2010 (ICES-WGEF 2019).

In the Mediterranean, the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM) banned demersal trawling below depths of >1,000 m in the Mediterranean Sea in 2005, however this is unlikely to provide any refuge for the Smallspotted Catshark. For European vessels fishing in Moroccan waters, there is a 5% bycatch limit for demersal sharks (European Commission 2020).
documentation.use_trade: The species is utilized for human consumption, fish meal, bait, or processed for oil. In the Mediterranean Sea, the species is often discarded (Abella et al. 2017).
documentation.rationale: The Smallspotted Catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula) is a small (to 100 cm total length) catshark found in the Northeast and Eastern Central Atlantic Ocean (from Norway and the British Isles to Senegal and possibly Benin) and the Mediterranean Sea. It occurs on the continental shelf and upper slope from nearshore to a depth of 800 m. The Smallspotted Catshark is reported as incidental catch in demersal trawl, longline, and gill net fisheries across its geographic and bathymetric range. It is now one of the most abundant elasmobranchs across its range in the Northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. In the Eastern Central Atlantic, sharks and rays have been exploited by semi-industrial fisheries since the 1950s. Off West Africa, there are a number of European distant-water vessels using demersal trawl and longline to target demersal fish and shrimp species that operate in the deeper depth limits of the species. There is high distribution overlap with fishing pressure, increasing population trends in some parts of its range, and some relevant management in its Northeast Atlantic range. There is no evidence of population decline, the species is not suspected to be close to reaching the population reduction threshold, and the Smallspotted Catshark is assessed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: This is the revised taxonomic concept for Scyliorhinus canicula, which now excludes Scyliorhinus duhamelii (Soares and de Carvalho 2019).
